newsitem.title: USA: U.S. very disappointed at collapse of Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. very disappointed at collapse of Zaire talks.

text.p: The United States said it was "very disappointed" that planned peace talks between Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila failed to take place Wednesday.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns urged the two men to make another attempt to arrange direct talks, saying a dispute over the venue could be resolved.
Wednesday's talks were cancelled when Kabila refused to board a South African ship in the Congolese port of Pointe Noire, U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun said.
"We're obviously very disappointed that the talks did not take place today," Burns told reporters. "We thought the talks were necessary to establish the conditions for an effective transition."
"We would encourage Mr Kabila and President Mobutu to find a way to speak to each other directly, or else we fear for future events...if there's not an agreement to work out a peaceful transition."

Sahnoun told reporters aboard the ship Kabila insisted at the last minute that the talks should take place in international waters, a demand rejected by South African President Nelson Mandela, who was to have chaired the meeting.
Burns declined to assign blame for the failure of the talks to take place, but said: "Surely this problem (of the venue) can be worked out."
The talks collapsed despite telephone calls Tuesday evening to Kabila and Mobutu by U.S. special envoy to Zaire Bill Richardson, now back in the United States, urging them both to attend.

Earlier, Burns told a news briefing that the United States planned no further reductions in its embassy staff in the Zaire capital Kinshasa despite the possibility that the city would be captured by rebel forces.
The original strength of some 50 U.S. diplomats in Kinshasa has been whittled down to 25, including ambassador Daniel Simpson, as the rebels have approached from the east.
"I can tell you that we do not anticipate drawing down any further our embassy staff in Kinshasa," Burns said.

"That is the core of our embassy staff and our objective is to keep that embassy open and fully operational throughout this crisis. Obviously, we will be looking at the security situation every day to assure ourselves that those people are protected."
Burns repeated appeals for the 325 private Americans still in Zaire to leave as soon as possible, although none have left for the past four days.
"If it is not peaceful, it is going to be violent. The rebel alliance is going to attack the capital city and all those Americans there are going to be in harm's way," he said.

"They may be chasing profits. They may think they are indispensible to their companies. They have got to think about their personal welfare. We cannot anticipate how the Zairean army itself is going to react to the transition."
Burns said later it was "really ill-advised" of the Americans not to leave.
